one_liner: Fractal Tree (Bε-tree) transactional key-value library behind TokuDB/TokuMX; beat MongoDB 2.2's B-tree indexes on out-of-RAM inserts.
what_it_does: PerconaFT is an embedded, transactional, crash-recoverable key-value engine. It builds as libft.so plus libtokuportability.so and exposes a Berkeley DB 4.6-style C API (DB_ENV, DB, DB_TXN, cursors), with an optional C++ wrapper (ftcxx). On top of the BDB shape it adds DB->update/update_broadcast upsert callbacks, a hot indexer, a bulk loader, snapshot, read-committed and serializable transactions, and range row locks through its locktree. It is not a MongoDB index plug-in: the 532x result came from Tokutek's own Fractal-Tree-indexed MongoDB build (the forerunner of TokuMX), which embedded this library.
how_it_is_fast: Every dictionary is a Fractal Tree, which is Tokutek's industrial Bε-tree (the buffered B-tree / cache-oblivious streaming B-tree family from Bender, Farach-Colton and Kuszmaul). Each internal node keeps one message buffer per child, ordered by key and message sequence number. Inserts, deletes (as tombstones) and upserts enter as messages near the root and are flushed down in batches to the fullest child, so one node I/O moves many updates instead of one random leaf read-modify-write per key. Nodes are large and compressed (4 MB default, fanout 16, leaves split into 128 KB basement nodes for partial reads, QuickLZ by default), and a promotion heuristic sends runs of sequential inserts straight to the rightmost leaf. In the benchmark, the 100-entry multikey index most likely outgrew 16 GB RAM, which forced MongoDB's B-tree into random disk reads per index entry. The fractal tree avoids those reads, though the blog post itself gives no cause.
when_to_use: Insert, delete or update-heavy workloads with several secondary indexes whose combined size is far beyond RAM on HDDs or bandwidth-limited SSDs, with random, high-cardinality keys. That is the regime of the 532x run and of Percona's 'up to two orders of magnitude' claim.

Blind updates such as counters, timestamps or balance deltas, written as DB->update upsert callbacks so no read-before-write is needed. The Bε-tree authors say upserts can speed updates up by one to two orders of magnitude.

An embedded transactional C/C++ key-value store with a Berkeley DB-like API, compressed on-disk nodes (QuickLZ, zlib, LZMA or Snappy) and hot index builds, on 64-bit Linux, where GPLv2/AGPLv3 is acceptable.
Keeping an existing TokuDB, TokuMX or Percona-FT deployment running, or studying a production-grade Bε-tree with checkpointing, logging and a range-lock manager.
when_not_to_use: Data or indexes that fit in RAM, or mostly sequential keys. Percona's docs say fractal trees only 'match B-trees' on sequential data. In Percona's own 2015 iiBench run (1B rows, 3 indexes, one SSD), WiredTiger's B-tree was fastest while data fit in memory, and RocksDB was 'overall better' than PerconaFT as data grew.

Read-before-write patterns such as unique-key checks and query-modify-insert. These run at point-query speed, which is no better than a B-tree, and every lookup must also apply pending messages buffered along the root-to-leaf path.

New projects that need an active upstream. The last commit was 2023-11-28 and GitHub issues are disabled. 28 PRs sit unmerged, including fsync error handling (#410, 2018), a crash when out of locks (#443), ThreadSanitizer-found data races (#396) and filesystems with non-512-byte sectors (#385). Percona dropped TokuDB as of Percona Server for MySQL 8.0.28-19 (2022-05-12).

Targets other than 64-bit Linux. 32-bit is unsupported, macOS and FreeBSD only 'may work' (macOS CI jobs were allowed to fail), and the cycle timer has #error for anything but x86, aarch64 and POWER. The s390x/RISC-V port PR is unmerged, and the TSan PR notes an x86 memory-model bias in the code.
Projects that need a permissive license. The core is GPLv2/AGPLv3 (only locktree and omt are Apache-2.0), and the PATENTS grant can be terminated if you challenge the patents.

integration.dependencies: zlib (system). Bundled in third_party: xz 4.999.9beta (LZMA), Snappy 1.1.2 and QuickLZ source. CMake >= 2.8.12. Valgrind is optional for tests.
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (-std=c++11) and C99. CI covered GCC 4.8-10 and Clang 4-10 on Ubuntu 18.04 (Travis). CMake 2.8.12+.
integration.platforms: 64-bit Linux (CentOS, Debian, Ubuntu supported). macOS 10.8 and FreeBSD 'may work'. No 32-bit. Timer code exists only for x86-64, aarch64 and POWER.
integration.thread_safety: Built for multi-threaded use: DB_THREAD handles, background cachetable, flusher and checkpoint thread pools, and a per-dictionary locktree with range row locks, wait-for-graph deadlock detection and lock timeouts. Caveat: an open PR (#396) reports about 100 unique ThreadSanitizer data-race and lock-order findings, and #447 reports a race on writing_rollback.

gotchas: It refuses to start when Linux transparent huge pages are enabled, because they break its memory accounting and can overcommit. TOKU_HUGE_PAGES_OK=1 overrides this, but the README says to use it only for testing with a small cache.
Under lock-memory pressure, DB->put can return TOKUDB_OUT_OF_LOCKS, and callers must handle it. The pending-lock retry path crashes in that case (PS-4328), and the fix is still an unmerged PR (#443).

Deletes are tombstone messages, so deleted rows and their space linger until the messages are flushed to the leaves. Compression failures assert instead of returning error codes (compress.h). The bundled xz is a 2009 beta.

The README build steps are stale (a jemalloc checkout, CMake 2.8.9, gcc47): CMakeLists.txt now requires 2.8.12 and no longer references jemalloc. The core is built with -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti, while the ftcxx wrapper throws ft_exception. TokuDB on-disk formats differ across MySQL variants, so moving between them takes a dump and reload.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over MyRocks, the LSM engine for MySQL that is still maintained, or over TidesDB and redb only if you specifically want an embeddable Berkeley DB-style transactional library with upsert messages for index-heavy, far-larger-than-RAM random writes, and you accept inheriting maintenance. The in-memory siblings (ALEX, HOT, Wormhole, the learned indexes) target a different, RAM-resident regime and are not substitutes.
verified_claims_summary: In Tokutek's 2012 vendor blog, MongoDB v2.2.RC0 loaded documents that each carried a 100-element array under a multikey index, so each insert meant 100 index operations. After 3.5M documents, stock MMAPv1 B-tree indexes had dropped to 2.11 inserts/s against 1,124.36 inserts/s for Tokutek's Fractal-Tree-indexed build. The machine was a Sun x4150 (2x Xeon 5460, 16 GB RAM, 4x10K SAS in RAID 0 behind a 256 MB write-back cache, Ubuntu 10.04, ext4). The figure is a single end-of-run 'exit velocity' point in a disk-bound regime, not an average, and no compiler flags are given. On HN a commenter noted that the stock curve had decayed to near zero, so the ratio depends on where the run stopped.
status_note: Stale: the last commit (2023-11-28) was a license fix, issues go to Percona's Jira rather than GitHub, and Percona dropped TokuDB from Percona Server 8.0.28-19 in 2022. The source can still be vendored and builds with CMake under GPLv2/AGPLv3 plus a patent grant, but you own all maintenance.
